topic: Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about how humans use the Earth's resources is correct?
items.correct: Earth's resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport
items.misconception: Earth's resources means the fuels and metals dug from rock
items.why: Mining and drilling are the images attached to the word, so living and atmospheric resources are left off the list. The specification says humans use the Earth's resources for warmth, shelter, food and transport, and that natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.
items.random_wrong: Farmed crops count as synthetic and not as resources

items.q: Natural resources are supplemented by agriculture. Which list of products does the specification give for these resources?
items.correct: Food, timber, clothing and fuels are all provided
items.misconception: Food and clothing only, since fuels are all synthetic
items.why: Mining and drilling are the images attached to the word, so living and atmospheric resources are left off the list. The specification says humans use the Earth's resources for warmth, shelter, food and transport, and that natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.
items.random_wrong: Warmth, shelter, transport and heavy machinery

items.q: Which pair correctly matches a natural product with the synthetic product that can replace it?
items.correct: Natural rubber from latex replaced by synthetic rubber
items.misconception: Natural cotton fibre is replaced by farmed wool fibre
items.why: Deliberate growing and industrial processing look man-made, so agricultural products get reclassified as synthetic. Synthetic products are made by chemical processes from other starting materials, such as polyester. Agriculture supplements natural supplies of a natural product; it does not turn cotton into a synthetic one.
items.random_wrong: Natural rubber from latex is replaced by iron and steel

items.q: Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed. What does the specification say this provides?
items.correct: Energy and the materials that people can use
items.misconception: Renewable supplies that will never be used up
items.why: 'Renew' sounds like 'reuse', and re-using a bottle is a far more familiar act than re-growing a forest. Renewable refers to the resource being re-formed in nature quickly enough to keep pace with demand, for example a replanted crop. Re-using an object is a separate idea.
items.random_wrong: Only fuels, since materials come from farming alone

items.q: What makes a resource finite rather than renewable?
items.correct: It is used up more quickly than it is replaced
items.misconception: It cannot be recycled after it has been used
items.why: Recycling is the sustainability idea students meet most often, so it becomes the test they apply to every resource question. Finite is about the rate of replacement, not about recycling. Metals are recyclable yet the ores they come from are still finite, because no new ore is forming on a useful timescale.
items.random_wrong: It is buried underground rather than grown

items.q: A student is given data on four materials. Which one should be classified as a renewable resource?
items.correct: Timber, because the trees felled are all replanted
items.misconception: Copper ore, because copper can be melted and reused
items.why: Recycling is the sustainability idea students meet most often, so it becomes the test they apply to every resource question. Finite is about the rate of replacement, not about recycling. Metals are recyclable yet the ores they come from are still finite, because no new ore is forming on a useful timescale.
items.random_wrong: Crude oil, because more is still being discovered

items.q: Which of these best describes sustainable development?
items.correct: Development that meets the needs of today without compromising future ones
items.misconception: Development that uses none of the natural resources of the Earth at all
items.why: Sustainability is presented in the media as cutting back, so students hear it as a ban rather than as a balance. The definition has two halves: current needs are still met, and future generations are not prevented from meeting theirs. Development continues; it is the way resources are used that changes.
items.random_wrong: Development that meets the needs of future generations rather than those of people now

items.q: What role does the specification say chemistry plays in the use of the Earth's resources?
items.correct: It improves agricultural and industrial processes
items.misconception: It replaces farming entirely with synthetic factory products
items.why: Deliberate growing and industrial processing look man-made, so agricultural products get reclassified as synthetic. Synthetic products are made by chemical processes from other starting materials, such as polyester. Agriculture supplements natural supplies of a natural product; it does not turn cotton into a synthetic one.
items.random_wrong: It removes the need to use finite resources at all

items.q: A table shows the volume of water used per person per day in four countries. Which conclusion can be drawn from the table alone?
items.correct: The country with the largest figure uses more per person than the others
items.misconception: The country with the largest figure uses the largest total volume
items.why: The heading 'per person per day' is skimmed and the figure is read as a plain amount, so the biggest number is taken to mean the biggest user. A per-person figure is a rate. It would have to be multiplied by the population to give a total, and the table gives no populations, so no total can be claimed from it.
items.random_wrong: The country using the least water per person has the driest climate

items.q: A river sample contains 12 mg/dm3 of dissolved solids; sea water contains about 35 000 mg/dm3. How do these compare?
items.correct: Sea water contains three orders of magnitude more
items.misconception: Sea water contains roughly three times as much
items.why: Students compare the leading digits and ignore the number of zeros, so a factor of a thousand reads as a factor of three. An order of magnitude is a factor of ten. 35 000 divided by 12 is about 3000, which is three orders of magnitude, not three times.
items.random_wrong: Sea water contains about ten times as much

items.q: Why is potable water not described as pure water in the chemical sense?
items.correct: Because it still contains some dissolved substances
items.misconception: Because pure water simply means water that is clean and safe
items.why: In everyday English 'pure' means clean or unspoilt, and bottled water is advertised as pure. Chemistry gives the word a much narrower meaning, met back in 4.1, that students rarely reconnect to drinking water. In chemistry pure means a single substance only. Evaporating tap water to dryness leaves a residue of dissolved salts, proving it is a mixture. Potable only means the levels of dissolved salts and microbes are low enough to be safe.
items.random_wrong: Because it has not been boiled before it is drunk

items.q: What does the specification say drinking water should have for humans?
items.correct: Low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
items.misconception: No dissolved salts and no microbes whatsoever in it
items.why: Students hear 'treatment' and assume the aim is total removal, and the word potable is often taught alongside purification. The specification says drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Low is not zero; mineral water is potable and is sold on the dissolved salts it contains.
items.random_wrong: Only water molecules, with everything else removed

items.q: Why do the methods used to produce potable water differ from one country to another?
items.correct: Because they depend on available supplies and local conditions
items.misconception: Because the same standard process is used in every country
items.why: A single treatment diagram is learnt, so it is taken to be universal rather than the UK case. Where fresh water is plentiful, filtering and sterilising is enough. Where fresh water is limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required.
items.random_wrong: Because sea water is the cheapest source in every country

items.q: In the UK, what is the first step in producing most potable water?
items.correct: Choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
items.misconception: Desalinating sea water taken from around the coast
items.why: Being surrounded by sea makes sea water feel like the obvious source, and desalination is the process students find most memorable. In the UK rain provides fresh water that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, so desalination is unnecessary. It is only required where supplies of fresh water are limited.
items.random_wrong: Adding chlorine into the water at the source

items.q: Why is water passed through filter beds during treatment?
items.correct: To remove the insoluble solids and large particles
items.misconception: To kill the microbes in the water before it is drunk
items.why: Filters are associated with 'cleaning', and students do not picture how much smaller a microbe is than a grain of sand. Filtration is a physical separation of insoluble solids. Microbes pass straight through, which is exactly why a separate sterilising step follows the filter beds.
items.random_wrong: To take the dissolved salts out of the water supply

items.q: What is achieved by the sterilising step in water treatment?
items.correct: Harmful microbes present in the water are killed
items.misconception: The grit and larger insoluble particles are taken out
items.why: Both steps are lumped together as 'cleaning the water', so their separate jobs are blurred. Each step has one job: filter beds remove insoluble solids, sterilising kills microbes. Chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light do not remove any solids.
items.random_wrong: The dissolved salts in the water are removed from it

items.q: Which set of sterilising agents for potable water is given in the specification?
items.correct: Chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light are all used
items.misconception: Chlorine and ozone only, as light adds nothing
items.why: Sterilising is assumed to mean dosing with a chemical, so a physical agent does not look like treatment at all. The specification names three sterilising agents: chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light. Ultraviolet light kills microbes without adding anything to the water.
items.random_wrong: Sand, gravel and fine activated charcoal beds

items.q: Which two methods of desalination does the specification name?
items.correct: Distillation, or a membrane process like reverse osmosis
items.misconception: Filtering through sand, then sterilising it with chlorine
items.why: Students treat filtration as a general-purpose purifier and forget that dissolved substances pass through filter paper and sand alike. Dissolved salts are in solution, so they pass through any filter. Removing them needs distillation or a membrane process such as reverse osmosis.
items.random_wrong: Crystallisation of the salt, followed by sedimentation

items.q: The UK has plentiful rain. Why is desalination not used to supply most of its potable water?
items.correct: Because desalination requires large amounts of energy
items.misconception: Because membranes cannot remove salt from sea water
items.why: The word 'reverse' is read as meaning everything happens backwards, including which substance crosses the membrane. The membrane is a barrier that water molecules can pass but dissolved ions cannot, so pure water is collected on the far side and concentrated salt solution is left behind.
items.random_wrong: Because sea water contains no dissolved salts in the UK

items.q: How does the treatment of salty water differ from the treatment of ground water?
items.correct: Salty water must have its dissolved salts removed
items.misconception: Salty water is filtered while ground water is only sterilised
items.why: Students treat filtration as a general-purpose purifier and forget that dissolved substances pass through filter paper and sand alike. Dissolved salts are in solution, so they pass through any filter. Removing them needs distillation or a membrane process such as reverse osmosis.
items.random_wrong: Ground water needs desalination but salty water does not

items.q: In Required practical 8, how is the mass of dissolved solids in a water sample found?
items.correct: By evaporating a set volume to dryness and weighing the residue
items.misconception: By measuring the pH of the water sample with a probe
items.why: Pure water is quoted as pH 7 in lessons, and students reverse the statement. Many neutral salt solutions have pH 7. Purity is tested by evaporating a measured volume to dryness and weighing any residue, not by pH alone.
items.random_wrong: By weighing the distillate collected during distillation

items.q: A student distils a sample of sea water in Required practical 8. What is collected in the receiving tube?
items.correct: Water that leaves no residue when it is evaporated
items.misconception: Sea water with all of its dissolved solids in it
items.why: Students picture everything in the flask travelling with the vapour, and do not separate boiling point from being carried along. Only water evaporates at the boiling point of the solution; the dissolved solids have far higher boiling points and remain in the flask. That is why the distillate has a pH near 7 and leaves no residue.
items.random_wrong: Salt solution that is more concentrated than before

items.q: Why may industrial waste water need treatment that sewage does not?
items.correct: Because it may contain harmful chemicals as well
items.misconception: Because it contains no organic matter at all
items.why: One treatment works is pictured as one process, and the contrast the specification draws between the two kinds of waste water is easy to skim past. The treatment matches the contaminants. Industrial waste water may contain harmful chemicals that domestic sewage does not, so it may require their removal as well.
items.random_wrong: Because it is always released straight into the rivers

items.q: What is the purpose of screening and grit removal at a sewage works?
items.correct: To remove large solid objects and the grit
items.misconception: To kill the harmful microbes present in the sewage
items.why: The first stage is assumed to be the most thorough one, and 'screening' suggests checking everything. Screening and grit removal is a coarse physical stage that takes out rags, sticks and grit. Microbes and organic matter are dealt with by the later biological stages.
items.random_wrong: To take the dissolved substances out of sewage

items.q: What two things does sedimentation produce during sewage treatment?
items.correct: Sewage sludge, which settles, and effluent above it
items.misconception: Solid effluent at the base and liquid sludge above
items.why: Both are unfamiliar words learnt as a pair, and neither sounds obviously solid or liquid. Sediment settles, so the sludge is the solid at the bottom. Effluent is what flows out, so it is the liquid.
items.random_wrong: Grit at the base and screened rags floating above

items.q: Which statement about the biological stages of sewage treatment is correct?
items.correct: Sludge is digested anaerobically and effluent treated aerobically
items.misconception: Sludge is treated aerobically and effluent anaerobically
items.why: The two words look alike and the two products appear in the same sentence, so the pairing is memorised the wrong way round. Sludge, the settled solid, goes to anaerobic digestion. Effluent, the liquid, goes to aerobic biological treatment. Anaerobic means without oxygen.
items.random_wrong: Both the sewage sludge and the effluent are digested anaerobically

items.q: Rank waste water, ground water and salt water by how easily potable water is obtained from them, easiest first.
items.correct: Ground water, then waste water, then salt water
items.misconception: Salt water first, then ground water, then waste water
items.why: Availability is confused with ease of treatment, and dissolved salt is invisible. Ease depends on what has to be removed. Ground water needs the least treatment, waste water needs more, and salty water needs desalination, which uses large amounts of energy.
items.random_wrong: Waste water, then salt water, and ground water last

items.q: Why are new methods of extracting copper from low-grade ores being developed?
items.correct: Because the copper ores left are becoming scarce
items.misconception: Because recycling means ore supplies can never run out
items.why: Recycling is presented as the answer to resource shortage, which makes the original supply feel unlimited. Recycling reuses metal already extracted; it creates no new ore. The specification states plainly that the Earth's resources of metal ores are limited.
items.random_wrong: Because low-grade ores give the highest yields of metal

items.q: Which statement describes phytomining?
items.correct: The plants absorb metal compounds and are then burned to give ash
items.misconception: Bacteria are used to make a leachate containing metal compounds
items.why: Bacteria are pictured as consuming things, and the word leaching is unfamiliar, so the product is guessed at. The bacteria produce a leachate, a solution containing dissolved metal compounds. Copper is then obtained from that solution by displacement or by electrolysis.
items.random_wrong: Plants absorb copper metal and store it in their leaves

items.q: What do the bacteria used in bioleaching produce?
items.correct: Leachate solutions containing metal compounds
items.misconception: Pure copper metal that is left behind in the rock
items.why: Bacteria are pictured as consuming things, and the word leaching is unfamiliar, so the product is guessed at. The bacteria produce a leachate, a solution containing dissolved metal compounds. Copper is then obtained from that solution by displacement or by electrolysis.
items.random_wrong: Ash containing the compounds of the metal

items.q: Scrap iron is added to a solution of a copper compound. What happens and why?
items.correct: Iron displaces the copper because iron is more reactive
items.misconception: The copper displaces the iron because copper is more reactive
items.why: Copper is a familiar, valuable metal, so students assume it must be the more reactive of the two. In the reactivity series iron is above copper. The more reactive metal goes into solution and the less reactive metal is displaced out, so iron dissolves and copper is deposited.
items.random_wrong: Nothing happens because the two metals are equally reactive

items.q: A student compares phytomining with traditional mining of copper. Which comparison is valid?
items.correct: Phytomining avoids moving large amounts of the rock
items.misconception: Phytomining yields pure copper metal without further processing
items.why: They are called methods of extracting copper, so students assume the metal is the immediate product. Both methods produce metal compounds. The compounds must then be processed, for example by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis, to obtain the metal.
items.random_wrong: Phytomining works best on the richest high-grade copper ores

items.q: How does the energy cost of desalination compare with treating fresh water?
items.correct: Desalination requires large amounts of energy, far more than filtering and sterilising fresh water.
items.misconception: Desalination is a cheap process because sea water is free and there is an unlimited supply of it.
items.why: The raw material being free is confused with the process being cheap, and the energy needed to boil or pressurise water is invisible. Distillation must boil the water, and reverse osmosis must force it through a membrane at high pressure. The specification states directly that these processes require large amounts of energy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What do the plants used in phytomining take up from the soil?
items.correct: Metal compounds, which end up in the ash when the harvested plants are burned.
items.misconception: The plants absorb pure copper metal and store it in their leaves.
items.why: 'Plants absorb the metal' is a convenient shorthand that hides the fact that copper is present in the ground as compounds. The copper in the ground is in compounds, and it is compounds that the plants absorb. Burning the plants gives ash containing metal compounds, which are then processed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are phytomining and bioleaching used?
items.correct: They allow copper to be extracted from low-grade ores as copper ores become scarce.
items.misconception: They are used on the richest ores because they give the highest yield of metal.
items.why: Newer methods are assumed to be better in every way, rather than being a response to the good ore running out. The specification links them to low-grade ores, which contain too little copper for traditional mining to be worthwhile, and to avoiding the digging, moving and disposal of large amounts of rock.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At which electrode is copper produced when a copper solution is electrolysed?
items.correct: At the negative electrode, because copper ions are positive.
items.misconception: Copper is produced at the positive electrode.
items.why: Students remember that copper is used as an electrode in the purification cell and lose track of which charge attracts the metal ions. Copper ions carry a positive charge, so they are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons and form copper metal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is timber a finite resource?
items.correct: No. Trees can be replanted and regrown, so timber is renewable.
items.misconception: Timber is finite because a tree that is cut down is gone for good.
items.why: The individual tree is the thing students picture, rather than the managed woodland that keeps replacing it. Finite and renewable describe the supply, not one object. Trees are replanted and regrow within a human lifetime, so timber is renewable, unlike crude oil.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does sustainable development mean putting future generations first?
items.correct: No. It meets the needs of current generations as well, without compromising future ones.
items.misconception: Sustainable development means giving up what we need now so that future generations have more.
items.why: The phrase 'future generations' is the memorable half of the definition, so the first half drops out. The definition is a balance of both: current needs are met, and the ability of future generations to meet their own needs is not compromised.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A table shows that country A uses the least water per person. What can be concluded?
items.correct: Only that its use per person is the lowest of those shown; the table gives no reason for it.
items.misconception: The country using the least water per person must be the one with the driest climate.
items.why: Students look for an explanation rather than a reading, and climate is the first cause that comes to mind, so a cause is read into a table that records none. Extracting information means stating what the figures show. A cause, a total or a future trend can only be claimed if the chart, graph or table actually contains that information.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water from a clean-looking lake safe to drink as it is?
items.correct: No. It must still be filtered and sterilised before it is potable.
items.misconception: Water from a clear lake or river is already potable because it looks clean.
items.why: Appearance is treated as evidence of safety, and microbes cannot be seen. Fresh water has low levels of dissolved substances but can still carry microbes. Choosing the source is only the first step; filtering and sterilising follow.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.1 Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water
